titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §195–214: an eye for an eye, and blows (xxxiii 41 – xxxiv 54)
part: Laws §195–214 · an eye for an eye & blows (Col. xxxiii 41 – xxxiv 54)
about: Twenty laws on striking and wounding: the stele’s “eye for an eye” block. A son who strikes his father has his hand cut off (§195; whether one hand or two is uncertain). Between men of the same rank the penalty is the injury itself: the eye destroyed, the bone broken, the tooth knocked out are repaid in kind (§196, §197, §200); but when the injured man is a commoner or a man’s slave the code asks silver instead (§198–199, §201). The blow to the face follows: a man who strikes the cheek of one greater than himself is flogged sixty strokes with an ox-hide whip in the assembly (§202); between equals the fine is one mina, between commoners ten shekels (§203–204); a slave who strikes a man’s son loses an ear (§205). Then the brawl: a man who wounds another in a quarrel swears that he did not do it knowingly and pays the physician (§206); if the man dies of the blow he swears and pays half a mina (for a man’s son) or a third of a mina (for a commoner’s son) (§207–208). The last six laws are about a pregnant woman struck so that she loses her child: ten shekels for a man’s daughter, five for a commoner’s, two for a slave-woman (§209, §211, §213); and if the woman herself dies, the striker’s own daughter is put to death (§210), or silver is paid, half a mina for a commoner’s daughter and a third of a mina for a slave-woman (§212, §214). The penalties are exactly as the stele states them. A few words (the two verbs of the eye clause, “cheek”, “brawl”, the two signs for “hand”, the sign group for “whip”) cannot be read with certainty; the notes say so each time.

sentences.i: If a son has struck his father,
sentences.n: The first of twenty laws on blows and wounds. §195–200 are the laws of the hand, the eye, the bone and the tooth (repaid in kind between equals, in silver otherwise), §201–205 the fines for a tooth and for a blow to the face, §206–208 the brawl, §209–214 the blow that makes a woman lose her child. Each is one “if” sentence, cut here at its verbs. šumma mārum abašu imtaḫaṣ is “if a-son his-father has-struck”: mārum is “son”, written with the single sign DUMU (Harper prints the ending -um, no ending is written on the plate); abašu is abum “father” in the accusative (-a-) with -šu “his”; imtaḫaṣ is the perfect (the infixed -ta-) of maḫāṣum “to strike”, the tense the code uses for a completed act in its “if” clause: “has struck”. The last sign of imtaḫaṣ is the AZ sign read aṣ, as everywhere in this part.

sentences.i: they shall cut off his hands.
sentences.n: The apodosis (the penalty): rittēšu inakkisū is “his-hands they-shall-cut-off”. inakkisū is the present, 3rd person plural, of nakāsum “to cut (off)”, with the plural ending -ū (written i-na-ak-ki-su, final sign SU as Harper prints it); a plural verb with no subject word is an impersonal “they”: the code does not say who does it, and the same form carries the penalties that follow (“they shall cut off”). rittēšu is two signs, UM and a vertical-and-bar sign that I key ME, then ŠU for -šu “his”; Harper’s list no. 65 gives UM + that sign as rittu “hand” and he normalizes rit-tê-šu. On the plate the second sign is a vertical wedge with a horizontal tail, the shape of his no. 184 me (his no. 181 lal is drawn alike), and his rittu entry shows UM followed by the same shape. The identification of the second sign is UNCERTAIN, and so is the number: -ē is a plural/dual ending in Harper’s normalization (“hands”); a single hand is possible. The penalty fits the offence: the hand that struck the father.

sentences.i: If a man has destroyed the eye of a man’s son,
sentences.n: §196, the most quoted law of the code. The talion laws are rendered from the grammar alone, and the same pattern runs through §196–200: a protasis with the perfect (“has done X to …”) and an apodosis with the present plural (“they shall do X to him”). šumma awīlum īn mār awīlim uḫtabbit is “if a-man the-eye-of a-man’s-son has-destroyed”. īn is īnum “eye” in the construct state (no ending, because a genitive follows), spelled i-in; mār awīlim is “a man’s son”, DUMU with the genitive awīlim: a member of the awīlum class, the code’s first rank. uḫtabbit is the perfect of the D-stem (the intensive; the u- is its mark) of ḫabātum, whose dictionary sense is “to rob, plunder”; “has destroyed” is taken from the sense of the law (the eye is lost), not derived from the grammar, which shows only an intensive of a verb of robbing. That it means “blinded” is likewise the sense of the law, not of the verb; the next unit puts the same eye on the offender. UNCERTAIN as a word.

sentences.i: they shall destroy his eye.
sentences.n: The talion itself: īnšu uḫappadū is “his-eye they-shall-destroy”. īnšu is īnum with -šu “his”; uḫappadū is a D-stem present, 3rd plural, of a verb ḫapādum, with the plural ending -ū. That verb is not met elsewhere in the code and I cannot confirm its meaning from the grammar; the sense “destroy” is taken from the law, where it must answer uḫtabbit above: the offender’s own eye is taken. The Akkadian has two different verbs (ḫabātum-D above, ḫapādum-D here); English “destroy” stands for both because the grammar does not tell them apart. UNCERTAIN as a word, plain as a law. House rendering of the pair: īn mār awīlim uḫtabbit … īnšu uḫappadū “has destroyed the eye of a man’s son … they shall destroy his eye”.

sentences.i: If he has broken a man’s bone,
sentences.n: §197, the bone. The law has no subject word (“he” is understood from §196). NER.PAD.DU is a three-sign Sumerogram: NER (Harper’s reading of the foot sign; modern editions read it GÌR), PAD, and DU; it stands for “bone”, Akkadian eṣemtum. Harper writes the logogram as it stands and I read it as eṣemti, the construct state before the genitive awīlim, with the ending supplied (none is written): the exact Akkadian form is UNCERTAIN, the word is not. Harper’s list no. 170 draws NER.PAD.DU as these three signs together. ištebir is the perfect of šebērum “to break” (iš-te-bi-ir): “has broken”. On the plate awīlim stands on a second tier (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.i: they shall break his bone.
sentences.n: eṣemtašu išebbirū is “his-bone they-shall-break”. NER.PAD.DU is followed here by ŠU (-šu “his”), so the Akkadian is eṣemta-šu, the accusative with the suffix (supplied; UNCERTAIN as above). išebbirū is the present, 3rd plural, of šebērum with the plural -ū (i-še-ib-bi-ru, the b of the present doubled). House rendering of the pair: eṣemti awīlim ištebir … eṣemtašu išebbirū “has broken a man’s bone … they shall break his bone”.

sentences.i: If he has destroyed the eye of a commoner
sentences.n: §198: the same injuries to a commoner. MAŠ.EN.KAK is the Sumerogram (three signs, MAŠ, EN, KAK, no ending written) for muškēnum, the commoner, the code’s second rank; the case is read from the sentence: here muškēnim, the genitive after the construct īn. The law changes its penalty: where §196–197 repay an injury to a man’s son in kind, an injury to a commoner is paid in silver. The sentence is in two halves (eye, then bone), joined by u lū “or”.

sentences.i: or has broken the bone of a commoner,
sentences.n: u lū is “or”: two words, ù (U3, “and”) and lu (lū “or indeed”), which the code writes apart; together they mean “or” (the pair is common in the earlier parts). eṣemti muškēnim ištebir is §197’s eṣemti … ištebir with muškēnim as the genitive: “has broken a commoner’s bone”. On the plate the line has MAŠ.EN.KAK on a second tier (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.i: he shall pay one mina of silver.
sentences.n: The penalty is a fine. išaqqal is the present of šaqālum “to weigh”, which is how silver is paid: “he shall pay”. The sum is ištēn mana kaspim, “one mina of silver”: the numeral is the single upright wedge DISH (said ištēn, “one”); mana is the mina (60 shekels, about half a kilogram) spelled with two syllable signs, ma-na (Harper prints ma-na in lower case; the plate shows two signs after the wedge); kaspim is kaspum “silver”, written KÙ.BABBAR: the two signs KÙ and BABBAR with no ending (on the plate only these two follow ma-na, here and in every silver line of this part); the -im of the genitive after mana is supplied by the grammar.

sentences.i: If he has destroyed the eye of a man’s slave
sentences.n: §199: the injury to a man’s slave. warad is the sign ARAD “slave” alone, Akkadian wardum in the construct state before awīlim (“a slave of a man”, the slave belongs to a member of the awīlum class); no ending is written. The rest is as in §198. On the plate warad awīlim stands on a second tier (Harper’s {b}).

sentences.i: or has broken the bone of a man’s slave,
sentences.n: As the second half of §198, with warad awīlim: “or (if) he has broken the bone of a man’s slave”. u lū “or”, eṣemti (NER.PAD.DU), ištebir.

sentences.i: he shall pay half of the slave’s price.
sentences.n: A slave is a possession, and the fine is a share of his price, not an eye or bone for his: mišil šīmišu išaqqal, “half of-his-price he-shall-weigh-out”. mišil is the construct of mišlum “half” (mi-ši-il); šīmišu is šīmum “price” with -šu “his”, written with the sign ŠÁM (Harper’s list no. 83 draws it as one long sign with hatched strokes inside) and ŠU; “his” is the slave’s. Harper prints šîmi-šu with a circumflex.

sentences.l: If a-man the-tooth-of a-man his-equal has-cast-out,
sentences.i: If a man has knocked out the tooth of a man who is his equal,
sentences.n: §200, the tooth. šumma awīlum šinni awīlim mēḫrišu ittadi is “if a-man the-tooth-of a-man his-equal has-cast-out”. šinni is šinnum “tooth” in the construct (ši-in-ni); mēḫrišu is mēḫrum “equal, counterpart” with -šu “his”: a man who stands level with the offender, as §203 says outright with ša kīma šuāti “who is like him”. ittadi is the perfect of nadûm “to cast, throw” (as in the code’s “to throw a body into the river”); of a tooth, “to knock out”: the verb is certain, the idiom is the law’s. Only between equals is the talion used; the lower ranks pay in silver (§201). House rendering: šinni awīlim mēḫrišu ittadi “has knocked out the tooth of a man who is his equal”.

sentences.i: they shall knock out his tooth.
sentences.n: šinnašu inaddû is “his-tooth they-shall-cast-out”: šinnašu is šinnum with -šu (ši-in-na-šu, accusative); inaddû is the present, 3rd plural, of nadûm (i-na-ad-du-u): the -û is the plural ending -ū joined to the weak final vowel of the verb. House rendering of the pair: šinni … ittadi … šinnašu inaddû “has knocked out the tooth … they shall knock out his tooth”.

sentences.i: If he has knocked out the tooth of a commoner,
sentences.n: §201: šumma šinni muškēnim ittadi, the same verb and noun as §200, with MAŠ.EN.KAK (muškēnim) as the genitive after the construct šinni; as in §198 there is no subject word, and no talion follows: the penalty is silver.

sentences.i: he shall pay one third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: šalšāt mana kaspim išaqqal: the first sign is the single fraction sign for ⅓ (Harper prints ⅓; the denominator is faint on the plate, and the Unicode character used is only the nearest single sign, as in the earlier parts: UNCERTAIN). The spoken form šalšāt “a third” is reconstructed. One third of a mina is twenty shekels.

sentences.l: If a-man the-cheek-of a-man who over-him is-great has-struck,
sentences.i: If a man has struck the cheek of a man who is greater than he,
sentences.n: §202 turns from limbs to the face, and to rank. šumma awīlum lēt awīlim ša elišu rabû imtaḫaṣ is “if a-man the-cheek-of a-man who over-him is-great has-struck”. lēt is lētum “cheek” (the dictionary sense “cheek, jaw”; UNCERTAIN, not derivable from the grammar) in the construct (li-e-it): the blow to the face is an insult of rank. ša elišu rabû is a relative clause: ša “who”, elišu “over him” (elī “over, above” + -šu), rabû “great” (the stative of rabûm “to be great” with the subjunctive ending -u that ša requires): “who is greater than he”, a man of higher standing. imtaḫaṣ as in §195.

sentences.i: he shall be struck sixty times in the assembly with an ox-hide whip.
sentences.n: The penalty is a public flogging. ina puḫrim is “in the assembly” (puḫrum, the same word as in §5; written pu-uḫ-ri-im, the BU sign read pu). ina qinazi alpim is “with a-whip of-an-ox”: the second ina is “by means of”; qinazi is written with the determinative mašak (KUŠ, hide, the SU sign) followed by a group of three touching pieces: a sprout-like sign, a cross and the box-and-triangle AZ. Harper’s list gives exactly this group as ONE sign, his no. 153 (value qinazu), and the plate’s first two pieces are not the ordinary KI and NA of the same plate (compare the KI of ak-ki-su and the NA of i-na). I keep a syllabic split, qi-na-az (keys KI, NA, AZ), as a reconstruction: the split, and with it the reading qi₂-na-az, is UNCERTAIN. qinazum “whip, thong” is the dictionary sense (UNCERTAIN, not derivable from the grammar) and the hide determinative marks leather; alpim “of an ox” is GU₄ alone (Harper’s list no. 109, the two bars and the triangle, one sign). The count is I ŠU.ŠI, “one ŠU.ŠI”: ŠU.ŠI is the word for sixty (šūši), so “sixty”; the thing counted (strokes) is not written. immaḫḫaṣ is the N-stem (the passive) present of maḫāṣum “to strike”: “he shall be struck” (im-maḫ-ḫa-aṣ).

sentences.l: If a-man’s-son the-cheek-of a-man’s-son who like-him has-struck,
sentences.i: If a man’s son has struck the cheek of a man’s son who is like himself,
sentences.n: §203: the same blow between equals. The subject is mār awīlim “a man’s son” where §202 has awīlum “a man”: the two ways of saying it are used side by side for a member of the awīlum class. ša kīma šuāti is another relative clause: kīma “like, as” + šuāti “that one, him” (oblique): “who is like him”, a man of the same rank; it is what mēḫrišu said in §200.

sentences.i: he shall pay one mina of silver.
sentences.n: The fine between equals is one mina, as for the commoner’s eye in §198: ištēn mana kaspim išaqqal (see §198 for the words).

sentences.i: If a commoner has struck the cheek of a commoner,
sentences.n: §204: between commoners. muškēnum (the subject, nominative) and muškēnim (the genitive) are both MAŠ.EN.KAK, bare; the case is read from the sentence. The first MAŠ.EN.KAK is the whole of line 88 after šumma.

sentences.i: he shall pay ten shekels of silver.
sentences.n: The fine is ten shekels, one sixth of the mina: ešret šiqil kaspim išaqqal. The numeral 10 is the single corner wedge (Harper prints X); ešret is the form of “ten” before a counted noun (the construct, as in the 10 GAN.E of the earlier parts; the feminine-looking numeral goes with a masculine noun such as šiqlum) and is reconstructed (UNCERTAIN, as for every spoken number). šiqil is šiqlum “shekel” (about 8.3 g) written with the sign GÍN.

sentences.l: If a-slave-of a-man the-cheek-of a-man’s-son has-struck,
sentences.i: If a man’s slave has struck the cheek of a man’s son,
sentences.n: §205: the slave who strikes a free man’s son. warad awīlim is the subject, “a man’s slave” (ARAD alone, as in §199); the victim is mār awīlim. The unit runs over from col. XXXIII into col. XXXIV (imtaḫaṣ is XXXIV 1). Where a free man pays silver for the blow (§203–204), the slave is punished on his body.

sentences.i: they shall cut off his ear.
sentences.n: uznašu inakkisū is “his-ear they-shall-cut-off”: uznašu is uznum “ear” in the accusative with -šu (u-zu-un-šu: U₂, ZU, UN, ŠU); inakkisū as in §195. One ear, as written: the noun has no plural ending.

sentences.i: If a man has struck another man in a brawl
sentences.n: §206 begins the laws of the brawl and the physician. A note on the numbers: from here to §221 Harper’s own §-headings in col. XXXIV run one line behind his running line numerals (his heading for §206 is XXXIV 4–12, his lines run 4–13); this edition follows the running numerals, which the plate’s margin numbers (5, 10, 15 …) match, and every line number here is theirs. šumma awīlum awīlam ina risbatim imtaḫaṣma is “if a-man a-man in-a-brawl has-struck, and”. awīlam is the accusative of awīlum, “another man” (the second a-wi-lam is on a second tier on the plate); risbatim is risbatum “brawl, quarrel” (ri-is-ba-tim, the sign is is, with plain s as Harper prints it; Harper’s sense; UNCERTAIN, the word is not met elsewhere); imtaḫaṣma is imtaḫaṣ with -ma “and”, joining this clause to the next.

sentences.i: and has set a wound on him,
sentences.n: ṣimmam ištakanšu is “a-wound he-has-set-on-him”: ṣimmam is ṣimmum “wound” (the sense is Harper’s, UNCERTAIN, not derivable from the grammar; accusative; Harper prints zi-im-ma-am here, with the sign ZI, and ṣi-im-ma-am at XXXV 21; I read the first syllable ṣi in both because the word is ṣimmum); ištakanšu is the perfect of šakānum “to place, set” with -šu(m) “on him, to him” (the dative suffix, written without its m): to set a wound on a man is to wound him.

sentences.l: that man in-knowing not I-struck-him he-shall-swear,
sentences.i: that man shall swear, “I did not strike him knowingly,”
sentences.n: awīlum šū ina idû lā amḫassu itamma: awīlum šū is “that man” (šū “that, he”); the oath that follows is quoted without a word for “saying”: ina idû lā amḫassu is “in knowing, not I-struck-him”, i.e. “I did not strike him knowingly”. idû is Harper’s i-du-u, taken as the infinitive of edûm “to know” after ina (UNCERTAIN as a parse, clear as sense); lā is “not”; amḫassu is amḫaṣ “I struck” (the 1st person preterite of maḫāṣum) + -šu “him”, the ṣ + š said ss and written with the ZU sign (am-ḫa-zu), as in the other parts (-ssu). itamma is the present of tamûm “to swear”: “he shall swear”. The oath clears him of intent; it does not clear him of the wound.

sentences.i: and he shall pay the physician.
sentences.n: u asâm ippal is “and the-physician he-shall-pay”. asâm is the Sumerogram A.ZU for asûm “physician” (the two signs A and ZU, no ending written, accusative); Harper reads the logogram so. ippal is the present of apālum “to answer, satisfy”, said of paying what is owed: “he shall pay”. On the plate u A.ZU stands on the first tier of line 13 and i-ip-pa-al on a second tier.

sentences.i: If the man has died from his blow, he shall swear, and
sentences.n: §207: when the man dies. šumma ina maḫāṣišu imtūt itammama is “if from-his-striking he-has-died, he-shall-swear, and”. maḫāṣišu is the infinitive of maḫāṣum “the striking” with -šu “his” (the striker’s blow); ina maḫāṣišu is “from his blow”. It is spelled ma-ḫa-zi-šu, the ZI sign read ṣi for the ṣ (and the word is broken across two tiers on the plate). imtūt is the perfect of mâtum “to die”, said of the man who was struck (his name is not written; the striker is the subject of itammama); itammama is itamma (§206) + -ma “and”: the same oath as in §206, and the sentence goes on.

sentences.l: if a-man’s-son, half mina of-silver he-shall-weigh-out.
sentences.i: if he was a man’s son, he shall pay half a mina of silver.
sentences.n: The second “if” is elliptical: šumma mār awīlim, “if (he was) a man’s son”; the penalty is mišil mana kaspim išaqqal. The first sign of the ½ is the cross-shaped MAŠ (Harper prints ½), which also stands for “half”; the spoken form mišil is the word of §199 and is reconstructed here.

sentences.l: If a-commoner’s-son, a-third mina of-silver he-shall-weigh-out.
sentences.i: If he was a commoner’s son, he shall pay one third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: §208 continues §207: šumma mār muškēnim, “if (he was) a commoner’s son”, with the lower fine, ⅓ mana kaspim išaqqal. It is a separate law only by Harper’s heading; the sentence is the same elliptical pair.

sentences.i: If a man has struck a man’s daughter
sentences.n: §209, the blow that makes a woman lose her child. šumma awīlum mārat awīlim imḫaṣma is “if a-man a-man’s-daughter has-struck, and”. mārat is the construct of mārtum “daughter”, written DUMU.SAL (DUMU and SAL, “woman”); imḫaṣma is imḫaṣ, the preterite of maḫāṣum (im-ḫa-aṣ), with -ma “and”.

sentences.i: and has made her lose what is in her womb,
sentences.n: ša libbiša uštaddīši is “that-of her-heart has-made-her-drop”. ša libbiša is “what is in her heart”: ša “that which”, libbum “heart, inner part, womb” with -ša “her”: the unborn child. uštaddīši is the perfect of the Š-stem (the causative) of nadûm “to throw, drop” with -ši “her”: “he has made her drop”, in the sense of miscarry. Harper prints uš-ta-dí-ši here, with an acute accent on the i (unexplained), and uš-ta-ad-di-ši at XXXIV 38 and 48: the same word, the geminate d spelled once or twice. No modern word for the fetus is used; the text does not have one.

sentences.l: ten shekels of-silver for that-of her-heart he-shall-weigh-out.
sentences.i: he shall pay ten shekels of silver for what was in her womb.
sentences.n: The fine is paid for the child she lost: ana ša libbiša “for what is in her womb” (ana “to, for”); ešret šiqil kaspim is as in §204 (X is the corner wedge for 10).

sentences.i: If that woman has died,
sentences.n: §210: if the woman herself dies. zinništum is the single sign SAL, “woman”, as in the earlier parts; šī is “that” (feminine, ši-i). imtūt “she has died” as in §207.

sentences.i: they shall kill his daughter.
sentences.n: mārassu idukkū is “his-daughter they-shall-kill”. mārassu is mārtum “daughter” with -šu “his” (DUMU.SAL, then ZU for -ssu: mārt + šu); “his” is the man who struck the woman. idukkū is the present, 3rd plural, of dâkum “to kill” (i-du-uk-ku; the sign for uk is Harper’s no. 62 ug, uk, drawn like his no. 63 az: key UG): “they shall kill”. This is the code’s measure for a death: the offender’s own daughter takes the place of the woman he killed. Never softened: the stele says kill.

sentences.l: If a-commoner’s-daughter by-a-striking that-of her-heart he-has-made-her-drop,
sentences.i: If he has made a commoner’s daughter lose what is in her womb by a blow,
sentences.n: §211, the same blow to a commoner’s daughter. There is no subject word and no verb of striking: mārat muškēnim ina maḫāṣim … uštaddīši is “a-commoner’s-daughter, by-a-striking, … has-made-her-drop”, the striker being understood from §209. maḫāṣim is the infinitive of maḫāṣum in the genitive after ina, “by a blow” (ma-ḫa-zi-im, ZI read ṣi; the word is broken across two lines on the plate). ša libbiša uštaddīši is as in §209 (here uš-ta-ad-di-ši, the d written twice).

sentences.i: he shall pay five shekels of silver.
sentences.n: ḫamšat šiqil kaspim išaqqal: V, the numeral 5 (five wedges in two groups), said ḫamšat (reconstructed, as the other spoken numbers); a commoner’s daughter is worth half the fine of a man’s daughter (§209).

sentences.i: If that woman has died,
sentences.n: §212: šumma zinništum šī imtūt, with šī spelled by a single sign (ši, Harper prints ši and not ši-i here, as the plate shows). The commoner’s daughter, if she dies.

sentences.i: he shall pay half a mina of silver.
sentences.n: mišil mana kaspim išaqqal, as in §207. The money replaces the death of §210: a commoner’s daughter is paid for, not repaid with a daughter.

sentences.i: If he has struck a man’s slave-woman
sentences.n: §213: the slave-woman. amat awīlim is “a man’s slave-woman”: amat is the construct of amtum, written GEME₂ (SAL and KUR, no ending); the sentence has no subject word. imḫaṣma as in §209.

sentences.i: and has made her lose what is in her womb,
sentences.n: As §209 and §211: ša libbiša uštaddīši (uš-ta-ad-di-ši).

sentences.i: he shall pay two shekels of silver.
sentences.n: šinā šiqil kaspim išaqqal: II is the numeral 2 (two wedges in one sign, said šinā, “two”).

sentences.i: If that slave-woman has died,
sentences.n: §214: šumma amtum šī imtūt: amtum, GEME₂ (SAL and KUR) as in §213, now the subject: “that slave-woman”.

sentences.i: he shall pay one third of a mina of silver.
sentences.n: šalšāt mana kaspim išaqqal, as in §201. Harper prints the first sign of the last word with a caron and a dot (iṣ̌aqal): a printing blemish; the plate shows I-ŠA-GAL, išaqqal, as in every other line. With this line the part ends (the next law begins at XXXIV 55).
